reasoning_summary: Step-by-step verification in order. 0003 correctly defines PCP yes-instances (the only quibble is leaving n >= 1 implicit in 'n in N'). 0005-0015 restate the target as 'c in C iff phi(c) is valid over all sigma-models', with phi = (phi1 ^ phi2) -> phi3 exactly as in Huth & Ryan. 0017 fixes the abbreviation f_s = f_{s_l} o ... o f_{s_1}, which is the book's convention and makes f_{uv}(x) = f_v(f_u(x)), the composition law the later induction needs. 0019 gives the intuition that phi1 and phi2 force P to hold on pairs (f_s(e), f_t(e)) coming from a common index sequence; the sentence 'then c in C iff exists z P(z,z)' is loosely stated (in an arbitrary model of phi1 ^ phi2, P may hold on extra pairs, so the right-to-left half of that biconditional is not available there), but the text explicitly hedges with 'perhaps in some other cases as well, but we won't care' and the argument that follows uses only the sound left-to-right half, so nothing load-bearing rests on the overstatement. 0021 correctly identifies that the direction under discussion (c in C => phi valid) must handle arbitrary models whose domain need not consist of strings, and that the 'interpret' function is exactly the map s |-> (f_s(e))^M into a subset of the domain; this answers the asked question and is mathematically right. 0023 completes the argument: from phi1 (base) and phi2 (inductive step, applicable because phi2 is universally quantified over domain elements) one gets (interpret(s_{i1}...s_{in}), interpret(t_{i1}...t_{in})) in P^M for every index sequence; if c in C pick a solution sequence, so s = t as strings, hence f_s(e) and f_t(e) are the same term and denote the same element z, giving P(z,z) and M |= phi3, hence M |= phi. The vacuous case (M not satisfying the antecedent) is handled implicitly by the conditional phrasing. Reached the end with no step certainly failing; the answer proves only the direction it explicitly scopes to, which is what the question asked about.
